text:
Tonight Anthony Davis played his first game in a Wizards uniform.

He put up 34 points, 11 rebounds, 4 assists and 2 steals in a Washington Wizards win over the Milwaukee Bucks. He made 11 of 20 in 33 minutes.

He is 33 years old, a ten time All Star, an NBA champion and one of the best defensive players of his generation. Before the game he said he wanted to go out there and showcase what I do.

Now go back eighteen years and look at the same person.

Anthony Davis grew up in Englewood on the South Side of Chicago and went to Perspectives Charter School, which is not a basketball school. It is a charter school. As a freshman he was 6 feet tall. As a junior he was 6 feet 3 inches, and he was a guard, and he was not being recruited by anybody.

He had exactly one Division I scholarship offer. Cleveland State, of the Horizon League.

Here is how he got it.

A referee who worked some of his high school games had sons who went to Cleveland State. That is the whole mechanism. Not a scouting service, not a showcase, not a highlight tape that found its way to the right desk. One official who happened to see him play and happened to have a family connection to one school.

In Davis's own words. "I knew a referee that used to ref some of our games and his sons went there."

That was the entire market for Anthony Davis.

Then his body did something almost nobody's body does. He grew seven inches. By his senior year he was 6 feet 10 inches, and crucially he had spent the years before that learning to play as a small man. Handle. Footwork. Perimeter instincts. He arrived at seven feet tall carrying a guard's toolkit, which is the reason he became what he became.

He played AAU for Mean Streets, the attention finally came the summer before his senior year, and inside a few months he went from one offer to the number one recruit in America.

He went to Kentucky for a single season. National championship. Most Outstanding Player of the Final Four. National Player of the Year. Then the New Orleans Hornets took him first overall in the 2012 draft, and he won Olympic gold that same summer at 19.

He has said the shot blocking that made him famous just came naturally, and that he had never really blocked shots before college. Think about that. The defensive skill he is known for worldwide is something he picked up after he was already the best prospect in the country.

What came after was a long and complicated career. Seven seasons in New Orleans. A championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020. Five All NBA teams, five All Defensive teams, ten All Star appearances. Then in February of 2025 he was the centrepiece of the strangest trade in modern NBA history, sent to the Dallas Mavericks for Luka Doncic. A year later Dallas moved him again, to the Washington Wizards.

The honest counterpoint. A hand injury wrecked his 2025-26 season, and since the start of 2024-25 he has missed more than 56% of the regular season games available to him. That is the number that actually matters, and one enormous October night does not move it. He is a 33 year old big man who has been traded twice in two years and whose body has been asked to do an extraordinary amount. And the growth spurt is the least earned part of this entire story. He did not work for those seven inches.

But he did work for everything he could do once he had them.

A 6 feet 3 inch guard at a charter school in Englewood got one scholarship offer in his life, and it came from a referee's family.

Tonight he was the best player on an NBA floor.

If you love basketball stories like these, follow us on any platform @ontaphoops

text:
A California wine business connected to Rep. Ilhan Omar's husband, Tim Mynett, is back under scrutiny after House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer made new allegations about its dealings with investors.

The company, eStCru, closed earlier this year.

But Comer says there's more.

During an appearance on Fox News, the Kentucky Republican alleged that investors were offered barrels of supposedly aged wine, only for those barrels to contain nothing.

That is a serious fraud allegation, but it has not been established in court.

The controversy also involves Omar's congressional financial disclosures.

In 2023, her husband's ownership stake in the winery was reported as being worth between $15,001 and $50,000.

A year later, the reported value jumped to between $1 million and $5 million.

Another business connected to Mynett, Rose Lake Capital, was listed at up to $25 million, bringing the combined reported value of the two business interests to as much as $30 million.

Those figures prompted questions from congressional investigators.

However, Omar subsequently amended her disclosures, substantially reducing the reported value of the holdings. Her office attributed the original figures to accounting errors involving business liabilities.

There's another development worth knowing.

A congressional ethics watchdog reviewed the financial-disclosure allegations and recommended dismissing them after finding insufficient reason to believe Omar had violated disclosure requirements.

That doesn't independently resolve the separate allegations involving winery investors.

But it does mean the original financial figures cannot simply be treated as proof that Omar or her husband committed fraud.

The winery has closed. Questions about its past dealings remain. And the alleged empty-barrel scheme has not been publicly proven.

🇺🇸 Should congressional financial disclosures involving multimillion-dollar business interests receive greater independent scrutiny, regardless of political party?

👇 What's your take?

text:
David, you've called me a TRAITOR repeatedly, yet you haven't demonstrated the courage or intellectual honesty to answer one simple question: WHY SHOULD I VOTE FOR DARLINE GRAHAM?

Not once have you explained what makes her more qualified than Ralph Norman. Not one substantive comparison of their records, accomplishments, constitutional principles, or qualifications. NOTHING.

Just accusations of treason because I refuse to vote the way you demand.

I served this country in the United States Navy. I've spent more than four decades involved in South Carolina politics, defending constitutional principles and challenging political establishments when I believed they were wrong.

And now you have the audacity to repeatedly call me a traitor because I won't surrender my conscience to the Graham political machine?

Let me educate you on something fundamental: MY LOYALTY IS TO THE UNITED STATES CONSTITUTION, NOT TO YOUR POLITICAL PREFERENCES.

Treason has an actual definition under Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution. Refusing to support your preferred candidate isn't remotely part of it.

Now, David, enough with the name-calling. Here's your opportunity to make an actual argument.

Tell me what Darline Graham has accomplished that makes her better qualified. Explain her record of defending constitutional government. Compare her qualifications, legislative experience, and demonstrated principles with Ralph Norman's.

MAKE YOUR CASE.

Because here's the bottom line: If the strongest argument you can offer for your candidate is to repeatedly call a fellow American a traitor for refusing to support her, you've made absolutely NO CASE for why she deserves my vote.

And understand something else: You don't get to define patriotism by obedience to a political party.

I didn't take an oath to Lindsey Graham, Donald Trump, or the Republican establishment. I took an oath to the Constitution.

I have never confused loyalty to my country with loyalty to a politician, and I have no intention of starting now.

STOP CALLING ME A TRAITOR AND START EXPLAINING WHY YOUR CANDIDATE DESERVES MY VOTE.

Surely that's not too much to ask.

text:
"Since that upper room experience on the eve of Gethsemane and Golgotha, children of the promise have been under covenant to remember Christ’s sacrifice in this newer, higher, more holy and personal way.

With a crust of bread, always broken, blessed, and offered first, we remember His bruised body and broken heart, His physical suffering on the cross where He cried, “I thirst,” and finally, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (John 19:28; Matt. 27:46).

With a small cup of water we remember the shedding of Christ’s blood and the depth of His spiritual suffering, anguish which began in the Garden of Gethsemane. There He said, “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). He was in agony and “prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luke 22:44).

That is why every ordinance of the gospel focuses in one way or another on the atonement of the Lord Jesus Christ, and surely that is why this particular ordinance with all its symbolism and imagery comes to us more readily and more repeatedly than any other in our life. It comes in what has been called “the most sacred, the most holy, of all the meetings of the Church” (Joseph Fielding Smith, Doctrines of Salvation, comp. Bruce R. McConkie, 3 vols. [Salt Lake City: Bookcraft, 1954–56], 2:340)."

President Jeffrey Roy Holland

text:
A LOT HAPPENED IN THE MARKETS TODAY. HERE'S A FULL RECAP:

1. Meta Platforms $META reported Q3 revenue of $64.60B, up 26% YoY, while net income rose to $9.86B from $2.71B a year earlier. Diluted EPS increased to $3.83 from $1.05. Operating income fell 37% to $12.99B, with operating margin dropping to 20% from 40%, partly due to a $9.89B legal charge related to its agreement with U.S. state attorneys general. Meta also reported negative free cash flow of $2.12B, its first negative quarter since 2012, as spending on AI infrastructure continued. On the earnings call, Zuckerberg said Muse AI had attracted more than 10 million users in six weeks, with roughly 25% using it daily. More than a quarter of active users are already shopping through Muse, spending over $200 per purchase on average.

 Zuckerberg said Meta expects more than 10x improvements in compute efficiency next year and believes Muse could eventually generate more revenue per user than its existing apps. Meta also announced an effective 2-for-1 stock split through the creation of nonvoting Class C shares. Existing shareholders will receive one Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they own, with the new share class taking effect on January 19, 2027. The structure will allow Meta to raise capital, compensate employees and fund acquisitions without reducing Zuckerberg's voting control.

2. Tesla $TSLA reported Q3 revenue of $28.05B, beating estimates of $27.88B, while adjusted EPS of $0.48 topped expectations of $0.43. Adjusted EBITDA reached $3.90B, above estimates of $3.71B, although operating income fell 56% YoY to $718M. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles during the quarter and reached the milestone of producing and delivering its 10 millionth vehicle. Active FSD subscriptions rose 67% YoY to 1.74 million, while cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles increased eightfold from the previous quarter. The company began offering Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3 and started Optimus production on high-volume lines in Fremont. Tesla Semi also entered volume production in Nevada, with its top variant offering 500 miles of range.

 Its Texas Megafactory began production with planned annual capacity of 50 GWh, while the Supercharger network expanded to 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors. On Terafab, Elon Musk said equipment commissioning is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with the first test chip targeted for May or June and useful chips at volume around Q3 2028. Musk also reiterated his belief that Optimus could eventually become the world's largest product category.

3. Anthropic is reportedly preparing to publicly release its S-1 IPO prospectus as early as Friday, October 23, according to people familiar with its plans. The company confidentially filed with the SEC in June and is reportedly targeting a November listing at a valuation potentially reaching $2T. A draft prospectus reviewed by The Wall Street Journal showed Anthropic generated $16.3B in revenue during the first half of 2026, compared with $1.1B a year earlier. The company also reported an $80.7B net loss, largely driven by a roughly $72B noncash accounting charge tied to convertible securities. Anthropic reportedly generated another $16.8B in revenue during Q3, up from $11.5B in Q2. Its draft filing also disclosed substantial long-term computing commitments and that two customers account for approximately 20% of revenue. Anthropic also introduced Claude Duet, an always-on personal AI agent powered by Opus 5.5, capable of managing emails, calendars, meetings, research and documents through more than 6,000 connectors and plugins. The company is opening a limited U.S. research preview for Claude Pro and Max subscribers.

4. Micron $MU laid out its memory roadmap through 2030, including plans for HBM4E in 2027, HBM5 and its first vertical HBM in 2028, HBM5E in 2029 and HBM6 in 2030. The company plans to begin offering customized HBM with HBM4E. Its next-generation 1δ DRAM process targets a mid-20% increase in bit density over 1γ, with U.S. manufacturing expected to ramp in the second half of 2027. Micron also plans to begin volume production of its G11 NAND in the second half of 2027, targeting more than 400 layers, roughly twice the bit density of G9, up to 1.5x faster I/O and over 25% lower energy use per bit. Future SSDs could reach 512TB, while high-IOPS NAND designs target 25M–100M small-block operations per second. Micron's CTO also told Nikkei that the company will stick with 6F² memory structures and next-generation 3D DRAM rather than pursuing 4F² designs, despite advances by Chinese competitor CXMT.

5. OpenAI expanded ChatGPT advertising to 26 additional countries, bringing the total to 89 countries worldwide. Alphabet $GOOGL fell approximately 2.6% on Wednesday, the same day OpenAI announced it was expanding ChatGPT advertising . The expansion puts OpenAI in more direct competition with Google's search advertising business, although it's unclear whether the announcement contributed to the decline.

6. Microsoft $MSFT reportedly attracted preliminary private equity interest in a potential $100B–$150B buyout of its Xbox gaming division, according to The Information. Several firms explored the possibility in recent months, but the discussions never reached Microsoft and no formal offers were made. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has denied that the business is for sale. Xbox's fiscal 2026 revenue reportedly fell 7% to $21.8B, with hardware sales down 29% and profit margins near 3%. The division is also reportedly considering cutting around 3,200 jobs from its workforce of approximately 14,000 and restructuring Game Pass subscriptions. Internal estimates for its next console, Project Helix, reportedly range from $1,200 to $1,800.

7. Unitree Robotics unveiled its H2-X humanoid robot, demonstrating martial arts, acrobatic movements and simulated security and rescue operations. The robot performed kicks, backflips and jumps from platforms approximately four meters high. Demonstration footage also showed it damaging car doors and lifting the front of a vehicle. Unitree claims up to eight hours of standing endurance, although that figure does not apply to continuous physical activity. 

8. Nvidia $NVDA announced several major developments at GTC Berlin, including DSX POD, a modular Vera Rubin AI factory design that could cut deployment time at a prepared site from six months to just 14 days. Nvidia is working with 17 partners, including Dell $DELL, HPE $HPE, Vertiv $VRT, Eaton $ETN and Foxconn, with deliveries expected in early 2027. The company also announced agreements with six manufacturers to expand semiconductor production, targeting a 2.5x increase in substrate capacity over three years. Amkor $AMKR plans to increase interposer wafer capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028, while Nvidia is providing KYEC with a $1.1B advance for new U.S. testing facilities. Nvidia also introduced new power and cooling technologies for AI data centers, including DSX MaxLPS software, which it says can generate the same number of AI tokens using up to 30% less power. During the keynote, Jensen Huang estimated that a 1 GW AI factory could cost around $50B and generate approximately $40B in annual revenue, meaning a three-month deployment delay could represent roughly $10B in lost revenue.

9. Elon Musk is reportedly pushing for a $3.7T merger between SpaceX and Tesla $TSLA, with an announcement targeted for the first half of 2027, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter. Musk reportedly wants the deal completed before President Trump leaves office. He has publicly called the combination a good idea, although no agreement has been reached, and special board committees are reviewing the proposal. Musk controls more than 80% of SpaceX's voting power but owns roughly 20% of Tesla, making approval from Tesla shareholders a major hurdle. The companies are already working together on AI, robotics and the Terafab semiconductor project. SpaceX shares have reportedly risen 47% since August 5, potentially making a stock-based transaction more attractive. Any merger would also face regulatory scrutiny because of SpaceX's U.S. defense contracts and Tesla's manufacturing operations in China. Bloomberg estimates the combination could increase Musk's personal fortune by more than $110B if completed.

10. U.S. stock futures fell Wednesday evening following earnings reports from Meta $META and Tesla $TSLA. Dow futures declined 0.31%, S&P 500 futures fell 0.40%, and Nasdaq-100 futures dropped 0.67%. Asian markets also traded lower, with Japan's Nikkei 225 down 0.40%, South Korea's Kospi falling 0.61%, and the Kosdaq losing 0.66%. Meanwhile, oil prices climbed, with WTI crude rising 0.91% to $98.03 per barrel and Brent crude gaining 1.09% to $110.01.

text:
The Biafra Self-Referendum: Organizing Independence from Exile Under International Law

In a detailed response to public questions, the Alliance of Biafran Americans explained the mechanics and legitimacy of a self-referendum for Biafran independence organized by PM Simon Ekpa and the Biafra Republic Government in Exile (BRGIE). 

It stated that the process was not an ad-hoc online exercise but one conducted both physically in the claimed Biafran homeland and electronically among the diaspora. It asserted that #Biafrans themselves authorized Ekpa to lead the effort after electing him Prime Minister at an assembly in Helsinki, Finland, in 2023.

The referendum is presented as a response to long-standing grievances. 

The accompanying quoted statement of Dr. Michael Rubin @mrubin1971 noted that

“Nigerian repression grew against ethnic Igbo in Biafra and Nigerian Christians more broadly,” framing the vote as an exercise of self-determination amid allegations of marginalization, insecurity, and ineffective governance. 

Organizers reported that tens of millions participated and overwhelmingly chose independence, with plans for a convention to declare the “Restoration of Independence of Biafra.” 

Dr. Rubin emphasized that holding aspects of the process in #Finland is not disqualifying, drawing a parallel to Czechoslovakia’s 1918 declaration of independence, which took place in Washington, D.C., rather than on Czech or Slovak soil.

On verification and international standards, the PAC stated that ORB International monitored the process on the ground and published a report. 

It further argued that United Nations involvement is not a legal prerequisite for a referendum on self-determination. While a state or entity may invite the UN, international law does not mandate it. 

ORB’s published commentary focused on public-opinion polling showing that residents of Biafra regions were among the most likely to view the national government as ineffective and to report feeling unsafe, providing contextual support for the organizers’ stated motivations even if it did not independently audit every ballot.

Under the 1933 Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States, an entity may claim the attributes of statehood by possessing a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. 

Article 3 of the Convention codifies the declarative theory: “The political existence of the state is independent of recognition by the other states.” 

Proponents of Biafran independence argue that a credible expression of popular will—through a referendum—helps demonstrate the existence of a permanent population seeking self-government and can support claims of an effective government and capacity for external relations, even if full international recognition remains a separate political question. 

Recognition is ultimately a discretionary act by existing states; meeting the Montevideo criteria is widely treated as a necessary but not always sufficient condition.

#Somaliland offers a relevant comparative example. After declaring independence in 1991, Somaliland held a constitutional referendum on 31 May 2001. Approximately 97 percent of those who voted approved the constitution, which affirmed independence. An international observer team from the Initiative and Referendum Institute concluded that the process was conducted “openly, fairly, honestly, and largely in accordance with internationally recognized election procedures,” despite limited participation in some contested areas. 

Somaliland has since maintained a functioning government, defined borders roughly corresponding to the former British Somaliland, and a permanent population, meeting the core Montevideo criteria in practice. https://t.co/ExgkQgiV34

text:
Global News Brief 
1. Globes: Teva shares rose 4.7% to $41.10, their highest level in nearly a decade, after the FDA approved Weltruza, a once-monthly under-the-skin injection of olanzapine for adults with schizophrenia. Teva said trials showed improvements in symptoms and functioning, while the formulation eliminates post-injection monitoring. The company estimates peak annual sales of $1.5 billion–$2 billion, and Jefferies raised its share-price target from $40 to $48 while maintaining a buy recommendation.

2. Financial Times: Brazil’s government is accelerating Bolsa Família welfare payments to 19 million households’ days before Sunday’s presidential run-off, as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva narrowly trails right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in polls. All October payments will arrive by Wednesday instead of being spread across the month’s final 10 days. The government says the change, effective through year-end, aims to help families cope with drought and flooding linked to an unusually strong El Niño.

3. Market Screener: Russian President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg to discuss new proposals for ending the Ukraine war and released American teacher Stephen Hubbard, who had been imprisoned on mercenary charges he denies. Witkoff brought ideas developed during talks with Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo, including security guarantees and postwar economic plans. The meeting came amid mounting US pressure on Kyiv and Ukrainian concerns over disruptions to American intelligence and satellite support, while Putin showed little willingness to compromise on Russia’s core demands.

4. Financial Times: Benjamin Netanyahu pushed for a major new offensive against Iran, with Israel preparing a multi-day bombing campaign for October 10 targeting power plants, nuclear facilities and regime sites, according to three people familiar with the plans. The operation was shelved because President Donald Trump opposed renewed fighting before the November 3 US midterm elections. Both leaders continue to threaten further strikes, while the planned campaign reportedly would have exceeded the intensity of the joint offensive launched in February.

5. The Business Daily: UAE minister of state Lana Nusseibeh is emerging as a potential late contender to succeed UN Secretary-General António Guterres, with supporters testing diplomatic backing as the succession race faces geopolitical deadlock. The former UAE ambassador to the UN could enter the contest as early as this week, diplomats say. Guterres steps down at the end of 2026, leaving a successor to confront a severe funding crisis, weakened international authority and US demands for deep cuts.

6. The Times of Israel: Dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refueling aircraft reportedly flew toward Iran’s border before turning back, with Israel telling Washington the mission was an exercise intended to deter Iranian attacks ahead of Israel’s election. Some unnamed US sources suspected it was intended to provoke Iranian fire and justify renewed strikes. Israeli security officials reportedly opposed unnecessary military action before the vote, while Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz issued fresh threats against Tehran amid heightened regional tensions.

7. Reuters: Elon Musk has backed a potential Tesla–SpaceX merger that could create a company worth about $3.5 trillion, combining electric vehicles, energy storage, robotics, satellite communications and space launches. The deal could coordinate investment, engineering and AI development while giving shareholders access to both businesses. However, it would face governance and regulatory hurdles, particularly because SpaceX serves US defense agencies while Tesla has extensive operations in China, and would combine several expensive, technically risky ventures under one company.

8. Yahoo Sports: The revamped Philadelphia 76ers showed early promise with a 106–100 season-opening victory over the defending champion Knicks, spoiling New York’s championship celebration. Tyrese Maxey led Philadelphia with 28 points, while newcomers Jaylen Brown added 19 points, eight rebounds and six assists, and LeBron James contributed 14 points, nine rebounds and seven assists. Despite uneven shooting and developing chemistry, Philadelphia’s scoring options and playmaking offered an encouraging glimpse of its potential as an Eastern Conference contender.

9. 1440 Daily Digest: Drone strikes killed at least 153 people at an outdoor market in Abyei, a disputed oil-rich region between Sudan and South Sudan, local officials said. Officials blamed the Sudanese army, with reports indicating the drones hit a fuel depot used by the rival Rapid Support Forces. text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, ​the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two.

The negotiations in a grand imperial palace in ‌St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia - the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher held in Russia whom US President Trump had asked the Kremlin chief to release.

Wednesday's encounter unfolded amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.

The latest talks also came more than ​two years since Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.

The Kremlin said the new 3-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take ​place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. They could begin sometime on or ⁠after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.

POSSIBLE MEETING BETWEEN TRUMP, PUTIN AND XI

Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, though Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was ​time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."

Putin also used Wednesday's talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it ​has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear programme. Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said.

Russia could also supply vast quantities of fertiliser to ‌the United ⁠States to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff.

A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history.

'NEW IDEAS'

Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no NATO membership for Kyiv, and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy, was also present at the talks with Witkoff and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, ​including some that were close to being realised.

Witkoff said ​he had brought some documents with him containing ⁠various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. 

Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone.

Zelenskiy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and ​Trump.

The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskiy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile.

FRAYING US-UKRAINE ​TIES

US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply ⁠since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections.

Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelenskiy said that Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those ⁠issues.

Citing US officials ​and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered ​the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has ​said he was not responsible and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

🚨 EXCEPTIONALLY LONG POST. 🚨

Because why not? 
What a beautiful way to wake up. 😭💜

Okay, Jungkook chose WAR last night😉🥰

I don't think people understand just how happy it makes me to see him sharing these beautiful pictures of Taehyung.
There is so much love in my heart for these two that moments like these leave me emotional in the most beautiful way.
I want them to live, laugh, make memories, and embrace every happiness life has to offer without feeling the need to explain themselves or seek anyone's approval.

They deserve that freedom.
They deserve that peace.
And they deserve to be happy simply because they are human beings who have every right to live life on their own terms. 🥹💚💜

And then I look at the comment section, and honestly, the audacity would be funny if it weren't so embarrassing.
The self-appointed authorities on Jungkook's life have arrived, convinced that their nasty comments and unsolicited opinions will somehow intimidate him into submission.

Sweetheart, who exactly told you that you have that kind of power over another human being?

Your disapproval is not a command, your bitterness is not a boundary, and your opinions are certainly not the centre of his universe.
Perhaps he simply wants to share what he wants to share and live as he wishes to live.
Whether the comments are open intentionally or not, one thing remains true: he does not owe anyone a smaller, quieter, more convenient version of himself just to make them comfortable.

Jungkook is allowed to live.

Taehyung is allowed to be cherished.

And neither of them needs anyone's permission to be happy. 💜💚

So, by all means, keep typing. Keep speculating. Keep exhausting yourselves trying to turn something beautiful into something ugly.

The sheer audacity of crawling into someone's comment section to vomit your bitterness, only to imagine that your unsolicited opinions carry any significance in his life, is quite something.
Imagine being so deeply bothered by another person's choices that you willingly embarrass yourself beneath his own post, mistaking your tantrums for influence and your hatred for relevance.🤣
Jungkook's Instagram is not a courtroom, your opinion is not a verdict, and you are certainly not important enough to dictate how he lives his life.

You are free to fill his comment section with your ugliness, just as I am free to look at these beautiful pictures with a heart overflowing with love for two people who have brought so much happiness into my life.
The difference? I leave with a heart full of affection; you leave having exposed the bitterness you carry within yourselves. And darling, no amount of nasty comments will make that look any less pathetic. 💜💚

You seem determined to find reasons to be unhappy about their lives, whereas I am simply grateful for every little glimpse of happiness they choose to share. You can keep searching for something to criticise, dissect, or turn into an argument.
Your negativity will never dictate the depth of my affection for them.

Jungkook, Taehyung, I hope life gives you both the freedom to follow your hearts, the peace to protect your happiness, and countless beautiful moments that belong to you and you alone.
I hope you laugh without restraint, live without fear, and never feel that you must justify your happiness to a world that will always have something to say.

My love for you both is not a demand, an expectation, or a condition.
I don't need you to prove anything, explain anything, or live up to anyone else's expectations.
I simply want you to be happy. Always. 💜💚

And to those busy policing another person's happiness,imagine having an entire life of your own and still choosing to spend your precious time being miserable about someone else's. What a terribly sad way to exist.

Let them live. I'll keep loving them. And you can keep seething, darling. We are clearly not here for the same reasons. 😂💜💚

text:
Sjoe! The Veto That Isn’t Written Down 🔐📓  ~  The Commission Got the Notebook. Who Hid the Key? ~ 🗝️ No Key, No Answers? 🔐📓The Madlanga Commission’s Secrecy Showdown.
Sjoe. The notebook arrives already locked. A commission created to examine what the country’s intelligence structures knew about organised-crime infiltration of the criminal justice system is told the pages that would answer the question may be opened only behind a closed door. 

The judge asks whether the holders of the notebook thereby decide the rules of the room. The reply is that the Commission was never given the key that would let it open the pages on any other terms. 

The veto is not written in the Commissions Act 8 of 1947. It appears in the space the Act left empty when it met a classification regime that is itself not a statute.

The Notebook Arrives Already Locked

On 21 October 2026 the Madlanga Commission sat in open session to hear argument on whether the testimony of Dr Ntandazo Sifolo, Acting Coordinator of the National Intelligence Coordinating Committee, together with the documents he was expected to address, must remain entirely closed. 

Those documents—four National Intelligence Estimates from 2022 to 2025, eleven intelligence briefs, and a special report covering January to July 2025—had been declassified solely for the Commission’s use. 

Evidence leader Advocate Matthew Chaskalson SC told the chair that the Commission “is not a high court” and “has no power to set aside a decision to classify information or to override a decision on the terms on which classified information is declassified” (Transcript of Madlanga Commission open argument, 21 October 2026). 

Justice Mbuyiseli Madlanga and Commissioner Sesi Baloyi tested the implication. Media counsel Advocate Ben Winks described the position as an ultimatum. The ruling was reserved for later announcement.

The claim tested here is narrow and falsifiable. A commission whose terms of reference require it to examine intelligence performance on the very infiltration alleged by Lieutenant-General Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi in July 2025 can still be left without the power to prevent the terms of limited declassification from controlling the hearing. 

The converging evidence draws from the Commission’s own transcript, the text of the 1947 Act, section 173 of the Constitution, the SARFU judgment, and the recorded practice of earlier inquiries. Each line is independent. 

Together they describe how a practical veto is produced rather than enacted.

Stirring Questions:
Does the absence of a power to override limited declassification already decide the form of the hearing, or does it merely set the opening position from which argument proceeds?
What additional showing, beyond the fact of classification, is still required before total closure follows?

What do these questions together establish? 
They locate the constraint in the tools the Commission was given rather than in any fresh decision to withhold, and they make the reserved ruling the moment at which that constraint either holds or yields.

Sjoe!
A key that was never cut cannot be lost. It can only be discovered missing when someone tries the lock.

What the Act Supplies and What It Leaves Empty

The Commissions Act 8 of 1947 authorises a presidential commission to summon witnesses, administer oaths and receive evidence. It does not confer the inherent jurisdiction a High Court exercises under section 173 of the Constitution to regulate its own process—including the power to commit for contempt in order to compel production or to vary the conditions on which evidence is received (Commissions Act 8 of 1947; Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, s 173). 

Classification decisions rest on the Minimum Information Security Standards. Winks submitted that these standards “is not a law” and that “there is no law on the statute books that provides for decisions to classify or declassify” (Transcript, 21 October 2026). Offence provisions in the Protection of Information Act 84 of 1982 and section 26 of the Intelligence Services Act 65 of 2002 nevertheless make unauthorised further dissemination a crime.

The constitutional design after 1994 treats open justice as the default in courts and expects restrictions to be justified by reference to the information itself. Commissions occupy a hybrid space: they are not courts, yet they investigate matters of public power and report to the President. 

The 1947 Act was drafted in a different constitutional order. It has not been revised to address either the open-justice expectation or the classification practices that grew up under the Minimum Information Security Standards. The practical result is a dependence on voluntary cooperation from the very institutions whose performance is under examination. 

When those institutions condition cooperation on total closure, the Act supplies no internal mechanism to refuse the condition.

Stirring Questions:
If the 1947 Act never contemplated a classification practice that could condition the supply of evidence, does the statute’s silence itself generate the veto once that practice appears?
What interim public account of the intelligence layer remains possible while the ruling is reserved?

What do these questions together establish? 
They shift attention from the motives of any participant to the design of the instrument that still governs the inquiry, and they ask whether an unrevised pre-constitutional statute can carry a post-constitutional mandate without producing exactly this gap.

Sjoe!
An Act written when the intelligence services answered to a different constitution is asked, nearly eighty years later, to referee a contest those services still largely define. 

The referee was never issued a whistle.

1. The Practical Veto

Chaskalson treated the missing section 173 power as decisive. He observed that the Commission also cannot imprison a party until documents are produced, pointing to the months of non-compliance by Suliman Carrim. Madlanga’s questions established that the evidence leaders had not sought Sifolo’s consent for any form of partial treatment. 

A senior state functionary can therefore condition the supply of evidence on total secrecy. The Commission must accept the condition or forgo the material. The veto requires no new regulation. It requires only that the 1947 Act continue to lack the tool that would allow the Commission to decline the condition while still obtaining the evidence.

The same structural feature appears whenever a state body under scrutiny controls the terms on which its records are released. The transcript does not create the feature; it records the moment the feature became the argument before the chair. 

Other witnesses have requested closed hearings and been refused when the justification was inadequate. The distinction drawn in argument is that those earlier requests typically rested on personal safety or informant protection—grounds that attach to the information itself—rather than on the bare fact of classification.

Stirring Questions:
Has the Commission previously refused an in-camera application grounded solely in classification rather than in personal safety or the protection of an informant?
If consent for partial treatment has not been sought, does the middle path remain open or has the practical range already narrowed?

What do these questions together establish? 
They test whether the veto is an absolute consequence of the Act or a position that has not yet been pressed to its limit inside this hearing.

Sjoe!
The Commission can subpoena a witness. It cannot subpoena the terms on which the witness’s documents will be allowed to speak. The difference is the entire argument.

2. The Non-Statutory Bar

Winks submitted that the Minimum Information Security Standards lack the character of law and therefore cannot bind the Commission’s process through the Oudekraal principle, under which an administrative decision ordinarily stands until set aside by a court (Oudekraal Estates (Pty) Ltd v City of Cape Town 2004 (6) SA 222 (SCA)). 

A classification decision, he argued, has no external legal effect that would compel another body to treat it as conclusive. Madlanga tested the contrary claim that limited declassification necessarily requires a closed hearing. The offence provisions remain in force. 

What is contested is whether those provisions, standing alone, convert a standards document into an automatic bar on the Commission’s ability to receive evidence in public.

The trajectory therefore moves from the Commission’s missing power to the legal character of the instrument that occupies the space the power would have filled. A High Court can, in the exercise of section 173, examine and if necessary override a classification for the purpose of its own proceedings. The Commission cannot. 

The reserved ruling must decide whether a non-statutory regime can perform the work the statute itself does not authorise, or whether the absence of statutory authorisation limits both the Commission and the classifier.

Stirring Questions:
If any intelligence body can classify or withdraw material at will, what prevents the same body from removing evidence from the Commission’s scrutiny altogether?
Does the absence of a classification statute limit the classifier as well as the Commission, or does it leave the classifier unconstrained while binding the inquiry?

What do these questions together establish? 
They ask whether the veto rests on positive law or on the continued absence of law, and they make the answer material to every future request for closed hearings on intelligence performance.

Sjoe!
A standards document that is not a law is asked to do the work of a statute. The document has no objection. The statute was never consulted.

2. Competing Institutional Memories

Winks placed the application beside the Harms Commission, in which intelligence and security structures were permitted to dictate what they would say and witnesses appeared in disguise, and beside the Goldstone Commission, which employed search and seizure. 

He submitted that a post-1994 inquiry should not revert to the earlier model. Chaskalson did not engage the comparison, confining his submissions to present statutory limits and the SARFU characterisation of function. The transcript thereby supplies a normative benchmark drawn from the country’s own institutional memory. 

Acceptance of total closure will be readable as continuity with a model later inquiries were understood to have left behind. Rejection will be readable as an assertion that the post-1994 departure still governs when the evidence concerns the performance of intelligence structures themselves.

The continuity is unremarked in the evidence leaders’ submissions. It is explicit in the media argument. Public trust is the stake Winks identified: a secret process that may influence recommendations the public never sees tested carries a legitimacy cost even if the recommendations are later published. 

The ruling will choose, by implication, which memory governs.

Stirring Questions:
Does the Harms record remain a caution only when personal safety is absent, or does it remain a caution whenever a state functionary conditions the supply of evidence on secrecy?
What measurable public-trust cost follows if later review shows that recommendations rested on a process the public was not permitted to observe?

What do these questions together establish?
They convert a technical dispute over powers into a legitimacy contest whose outcome will be read against the country’s prior experience of intelligence structures dictating terms to inquiries.

Sjoe!
The disguises of the Harms era were visible. The present argument wears a statute. Both achieve the same result if the statute contains no contrary power.

3. The Advisory Hierarchy

Chaskalson cited the SARFU judgment to locate the Commission’s purpose: a commission “is an adjunct to the policy formation responsibility of the president” and exists to obtain information and advice, not to provide “daytime television” (President of the Republic of South Africa v South African Rugby Football Union 2000 (1) SA 1 (CC)). 

Public interest in the material is acknowledged but treated as secondary to the ability to receive the evidence on the conditions under which it was offered. The media reply treated visible examination of what intelligence structures knew and reported about infiltration as necessary to the legitimacy of any advice that follows.

Building on the historical contrast, the hierarchy asks whether open justice can be subordinated when the information in question is the institutional performance the Commission’s own terms of reference require it to examine. 

The body established for accountability is invited to treat public access as optional once private advice can still be obtained. SARFU describes the ultimate destination of a commission’s work. It does not, on the argument advanced by Winks, extinguish the requirement that restrictions on the process be justified by reference to the specific information when that information goes to the heart of the mandate.

Stirring Questions:
If the primary task is advice to the President, what minimum public account of the intelligence layer is still required for that advice to be understood as having tested the mandate?
Does the SARFU characterisation limit the Commission’s process, or does it only describe the purpose to which the process is directed?

What do these questions together establish? 
They decide whether the public is entitled to observe the examination or only to receive the recommendation that results from an examination it did not see.

Sjoe!
Advice given in private may be excellent. Advice whose premises the public cannot inspect is advice whose excellence the public must take on trust. The Commission was not established to increase the volume of things taken on trust.

4. The Unactivated Middle Path

The transcript records that consent for any form of partial disclosure had not been sought. Chaskalson suggested that the appropriate next step was to return and seek such consent rather than to make an order binding on Sifolo. Madlanga reserved the ruling for announcement through the spokesperson. 

The only non-adjudicative route identified during the hearing therefore remains untested. Any future public record of the intelligence layer will depend either on that ruling or on voluntary cooperation that has not yet been requested. The available routes have narrowed to those two.

Partial treatment—redaction of operational detail, codenames, closed sessions limited to specific passages—has been used in other proceedings where the justification attached to identifiable risks. The transcript does not show that such separation was attempted here before the application for total closure was brought. 

The middle path exists on the record of the argument and has not been walked.

Stirring Questions:
If consent is now sought and refused, does the characterisation of the position as an ultimatum become complete?
What form of partial record—redacted estimates, codenamed briefs, or closed sessions confined to operational method—would still permit the public to assess whether knowledge of infiltration existed and whether it was acted upon?

What do these questions together establish? 
They identify the last procedural step that does not require the Commission to exercise a power it maintains it lacks, and they make the failure to take that step part of the record against which the reserved ruling will be read.

Sjoe!
A door that can be opened a crack is not the same as a door that must remain shut. The crack has been described. No one has yet tried the handle.

Synthesis

The lines of evidence converge without circularity. The 1947 Act supplies no section 173 power to override the terms of limited declassification or to compel production by contempt. The classification regime that occupies the resulting space is contested as non-statutory. 

Historical practice supplies a benchmark against which acceptance of dictated terms will be measured. The SARFU framing treats public access as secondary to the advisory function. The only identified middle path remains unactivated. 

Each observation is independent of the others; each reinforces the description of a veto that is produced by silence rather than enacted by text.

The claim remains falsifiable. A ruling that orders a workable form of partial openness, or a subsequent consent that yields a public record sufficient to assess institutional knowledge and response, would demonstrate that the veto was not structural. 

Until one of those events occurs, the cumulative effect of the missing provisions is that the terms attached to the documents control the hearing. The stake is the public’s ability to see whether the coordinating structures possessed, reported and acted upon knowledge of the infiltration the Commission was established to examine.

Objections

The material may be so interwoven that any separation would destroy its evidentiary value. The transcript records the assertion. It also records that consent for any attempt at separation has not been sought, so the practical impossibility remains untested. 

National security may require total closure in this instance. Prior in-camera orders have been granted where personal safety or informant protection was shown; the hearing distinguished those grounds from reliance on classification alone, and the chair examined the distinction. 

The Commission’s advisory role may properly limit publicity. SARFU describes the destination of the work. It does not, on the record of the argument, remove the expectation that restrictions on process be justified by the character of the information when the information is the performance under the terms of reference. 

Conclusion

A commission can receive the mandate and still be left without the key. The veto is not contained in any single section of the 1947 Act. It is produced by the Act’s continued silence when that silence encounters a classification practice whose statutory foundation is contested, a historical memory that treated dictated terms as a failure to be left behind, an advisory characterisation that treats publicity as secondary, and a middle path that was identified in argument and not activated. 

The public record of what the coordinating structures knew will therefore be partial by later ruling, partial by consent, or absent. None of those outcomes is compelled by an express prohibition. 

Each is the result of powers that were never conferred and steps that were never taken. 

Sjoe. 
The notebook is in the room. The lock is real. The key was never made.

WAR

Russian drone and missile strikes on energy sites caused new power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions, including Lviv, Rivne and Ternopil in the west.
Industrial power limits were imposed nationwide, per Ukrenergo.

Zelensky said US intelligence and early warnings on Russian ballistic missiles were restored after a week without them.

A US official called the Oslo talks with Zelensky and European leaders constructive.
Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg on Oct 21.
Russia released US detainee Stephen Hubbard.
Putin agreed in principle to US-Russia-Ukraine talks around Nov 10, possibly in Abu Dhabi.
Trump said it is time for Ukraine to end the war.

Iranian President Pezeshkian told Pakistan's army chief Munir in Tehran that Iran will not talk with Washington until US threats, sanctions and the blockade are lifted.
Iranian officials said enriched uranium stays in Iran.

Foreign Minister Araqchi said Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have not answered Iran's offer to broker peace talks.
A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran, per Nournews.

Iran said US forces struck its Konarak naval base and wounded two personnel.
US officials denied this, and also denied the IRGC claim that it shot down an MQ-9 drone.

IRGC spokesman Hossein Mojabi threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Gulf and Hormuz.
He said new weapons will be unveiled.

The Houthis claimed strikes on an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, and the Riyadh and Abha airports.
Saudi Arabia has not confirmed them.

MACRO

text:
Me: The art of using color when advertising

Ai: Color is one of the most powerful tools in advertising—it shapes first impressions, triggers emotions, guides attention, and can dramatically influence whether someone notices, trusts, or acts on your message.
Studies consistently show that color influences up to 90% of snap judgments about products, and roughly 85% of purchase decisions are influenced by color alone. Color ads are read about 42% more often than black-and-white ones, and consistent use of color can boost brand recognition by as much as 80%.

Red CTAs often outperform green or blue ones (sometimes by 20–34% in CTR tests) because they create urgency and stand out. Warm colors (red/orange) tend to drive action, while cool colors (blue/green) build trust.

Core Principles for Effective Use
1. The 60-30-10 Rule
This is the most reliable framework for balanced, high-performing ads:
•  60% Dominant color (sets the mood—often a background or large area)
•  30% Secondary color (supports and adds interest)
•  10% Accent color (CTAs, key highlights, the element you want the eye to land on)
Palettes with 3–4 colors generally outperform both monochromatic and overly complex ones.
2. Contrast is non-negotiable
High contrast makes ads more visible and readable. Aim for strong contrast between text/CTAs and their backgrounds (WCAG guidelines suggest at least 4.5:1 for body text). High-contrast combinations can boost visibility and stopping power significantly.
3. Align with brand and campaign goal
•  Urgency/sales → warm colors + strong contrast
•  Trust/awareness → blues, greens, or consistent brand colors
•  Luxury → black, deep jewel tones, gold, or restrained palettes
Your ad colors should reinforce (or deliberately contrast with) your brand identity. Inconsistency weakens recognition.
4. Color schemes from the color wheel
•  Complementary (opposites, e.g., blue + orange): High energy and contrast—great for CTAs
•  Analogous (neighbors, e.g., blue-teal-green): Harmonious and calming
•  Monochromatic: Sophisticated and luxurious when done well

Practical Tips
•  Reserve the most contrasting, attention-grabbing color for your CTA. Red or orange on a neutral or cool background is a classic high-performer.
•  Use white space strategically—cluttered color schemes reduce comprehension.
•  Consider the platform: What blends into a feed versus what stops the scroll.
•  Cultural context matters. Red signals luck and prosperity in much of East Asia but urgency or danger in many Western contexts. White is pure in the West and associated with mourning in some Asian cultures.
•  Test ruthlessly. A/B test CTA colors, backgrounds, and overall palettes. What works for one audience or offer can fail for another.
•  Keep accessibility in mind—sufficient contrast helps everyone, including people with color vision deficiencies.

Classic Examples
•  Coca-Cola: Dominant red for energy, appetite, and instant recognition (paired with white for clarity).
•  McDonald’s: Red + yellow combination stimulates appetite and feels cheerful/value-oriented.
•  Blue-dominated finance and tech brands: Project trust and stability.
•  Luxury brands: Often lean into black, white, or deep muted tones with gold accents for sophistication.

Army has spent the first half of 2031 proving it can win almost every kind of football game.
Now comes one where records matter a little less.

This is Army–Air Force.
This is academy football.
And this is the next step in the fight for the Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy.

THE QUICK HIT — THE TROPHY ROAD BEGINS HERE

Operation Blackout arrives at Air Force at 6–0, ranked #5 in the College Football Playoff, and coming off perhaps its most revealing win of the season: a 48–31 road victory over Tulane.

Air Force enters at 2–5 (1–3).

On paper, Army owns the stronger résumé.

On Saturday, that guarantees absolutely nothing.

Service-academy games bring familiarity, discipline and rivalry pressure that can erase advantages quickly. Army doesn't need style points here nearly as much as it needs control.

Beat Air Force.

Move to 7–0.

Then keep the path toward Navy — and the Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy — firmly in Army's hands.

Operation Blackout has national-title goals. This week, however, the mission is much older than the playoff.

HSN FILM ROOM

Army's transformation under Coach Hawk has reached the point where the Black Knights no longer have to win one specific way.

Against Boise State, they survived.

Against Colorado, they suffocated an opponent 48–0.

Against Florida Atlantic, they rolled 41–7.

Against Rice, they detonated for 63 points.

Then Tulane forced Army into a completely different game.

The Black Knights answered with 27 fourth-quarter points in a 48–31 victory.

That matters entering this rivalry because Air Force knows Army better than almost anyone on the schedule. There are fewer schematic surprises between service academies. Personnel discipline, leverage and execution become even more important.

Army's advantage is that this version of Operation Blackout has developed considerably beyond a one-dimensional identity.

THE BACKFIELD IS BECOMING A PROBLEM

K.J. Cruise remains the foundation.

But he isn't alone anymore.

Against Tulane, Cruise carried 12 times for 55 yards and a touchdown while Kevin Gutierrez added 52 yards and two scores.

Army also produced explosive runs from J. Procter and quarterback D. Berryman, each breaking a 44-yarder.

That diversity changes how Air Force has to defend the Black Knights.

Key on Cruise too aggressively and someone else can punish the edge.

Overcommit numbers to the box and Army has already shown it can throw behind you.

That is much different from simply preparing for one featured runner.

ARMY'S QUARTERBACK SITUATION IS BECOMING A WEAPON

The Tulane game offered perhaps the clearest evidence yet.

D. Berryman: 9-of-14, 135 yards, 2 TD, 0 INT
I. Ha: 8-of-10, 103 yards, 1 TD, 0 INT

Combined:

17-of-24 | 238 yards | 3 TD | 0 INT

Army doesn't need either quarterback to become a volume passer.

It needs efficiency.

Make the correct read.

Punish loaded boxes.

Protect the football.

Hit explosives when defenses start selling out against the run.

Against Tulane, that formula worked almost perfectly.
DOMINIQUE CARTER CHANGES THE FIELD EVEN WITHOUT CATCHING A TOUCHDOWN

Carter's Week 9 stat line tells the story of how difficult he has become to contain.

He caught 6 passes for 87 yards.
Then he added 174 kick-return yards, including a 98-yard touchdown.
That's 261 all-purpose yards.
Air Force can play good defense and still lose field position because Carter touches the football.

That creates a brutal problem for an underdog.

Long offensive drives become more important because every kickoff potentially gives Army another opportunity to flip the field instantly.

And when Carter doesn't get the football, his presence still changes coverage.

THE DEFENSIVE CHALLENGE

Army's defense has carried this team for much of 2031, but Tulane showed that opponents can move the football.

Tulane generated 445 total yards and ran 70 plays.

The important number was two.

Two Army interceptions.

D. Garnes grabbed one.

J. Lobato grabbed another.

Army committed zero turnovers.

That's winning football even when the defense isn't producing a shutdown.

Against Air Force, discipline becomes everything.

Academy offenses punish defenders for freelancing. One missed assignment can turn a routine play into an explosive one.

The Black Knights don't need hero football defensively.

They need assignment football.

THE COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF’S TROPHY PICTURE

This is where Saturday becomes bigger than Army's 6–0 record.

The Commander-in-Chief's Trophy belongs to the service-academy rivalry series between Army, Air Force and Navy.

Army still has Navy waiting at the end of the regular season, so beating Air Force would not finish the job by itself.

It would put Army in position to finish it.

Lose here and the equation becomes more complicated.

Win here and the mission becomes simple:

Beat Navy.

That gives this game two completely different layers.

There is the national layer — Army trying to protect a #5 CFP position and remain unbeaten.

Then there is the academy layer — something rankings cannot replace.

Coach Hawk can chase championships and playoff trophies.

The Commander-in-Chief's Trophy is personal.

WHAT AIR FORCE CAN DO TO MAKE THIS UGLY

Air Force's 2–5 record makes Army the obvious favorite.

The biggest danger is treating that record like an accurate representation of what rivalry football will feel like.

Air Force's path is straightforward: shorten the game, control possession, force Army into long-yardage situations and prevent explosive plays.

The longer this remains a one-score game, the more pressure shifts toward Army.

Army's answer should be aggression without recklessness.

Establish Cruise.

Get Gutierrez involved.

Make Air Force defend both quarterbacks.

Find Carter in space.

And above everything else:

Don't give Air Force extra possessions.

HSN KEYS TO OPERATION BLACKOUT

Win first down. Academy games become uncomfortable when offenses consistently stay ahead of schedule.

Protect the football. Army was turnover-free against Tulane. That needs to continue.

Make Air Force defend the entire roster. Cruise is the centerpiece, not the entire offense.

Force Air Force to chase points. Army's roster becomes far more dangerous when an opponent has to abandon its preferred pace.

Treat the rivalry like the rivalry. Forget 6–0 versus 2–5 once the ball is kicked.

HSN FINAL WORD

Six games have produced six wins.

Army is now #5 in the playoff rankings.

Operation Blackout has moved beyond being an interesting rebuild and into the national championship conversation.

But programs at West Point are not measured solely by polls.

Some games carry their own currency.

Air Force is one of them.

The Falcons can damage Army's perfect season.

They can complicate the Commander-in-Chief's Trophy race.

And they can force Coach Hawk's team into exactly the kind of uncomfortable football that rankings don't account for.

Army has the better record.

Army has the deeper résumé.

Army has looked like the better football team.

Now the Black Knights have to prove it in an academy rivalry where none of that matters once the opening kick goes into the air.

MISSION: AIR FORCE.

OBJECTIVE: 7–0.

TROPHY STATUS: ONE STEP CLOSER.

OPERATION BLACKOUT CONTINUES.

text:
A wonderful slice of Americana🇺🇸in Elko, Nevada. The Star Hotel & Bar, Basque Dining.

Outside of a mining conference, I've never seen so many mining contractors and core drillers in one place.

Check out the history of The Star, a fusion of Spanish & French roots transported to the American West:

"The Star Hotel opened in December of 1910 after a September construction start and building costs of $11,000. The long time dream of Pete Jauregui to make a home away from home for Basques, had come true. Eleven rooms, one bath and heat from wood stoves provided a cozy home for herders needing a place to stay until spring. Two years later, increased business demands required adding on, thus doubling the size of the building to its present day size. Sheep bands were sold in the winter, leaving herders without a home. The Star Hotel offered a friendly place with familiar language and customs, so unlike the English language and the incomprehensible customs they found in their new, strange land.

The Basques, since recorded time, have always sought work wherever necessary to survive economically. Whether they were cod fishermen in Newfoundland prior to Leif Erickson, Europe’s first whalers, or sailors Columbus relied on, they never forgot their homeland. It was customary for Basques to immigrate and then, once established, bring over family. It was common for religious people to immigrate, as evidenced in Mexico, which at the time included the American Southwest, California, and Nevada. The first bishop and archbishop of Mexico were Basque and influenced Basques to colonize the territory.

Many Basques went to South America, and not until the 49’ers and the gold rush in the late 1840’s did the Basques send word of their new land. They brought relatives to be ranchers and sheepherders, and as the word and idea spread, many Basques came and were among the primary developers of the open-range sheep industry.

Time and political wars divided the Basques geographically—the North, France; the South, Spain ~ “Zazpiak bat,” “the Seven are One,” symbolizes the four Spanish provinces and the three French provinces. The beginning of Basque nationalism and the name “Euskadi,” referring to the Basque region, began in the 1890’s. It was a long time coming for a group of people and a language that evolved from the inhabitants of the caves of that region over 10,000 years ago.

The Star Hotel was and continues to be a gathering place for all Basques. When it was first built, nightlife was nonexistent and the Star began holding dances, forerunners to the Sheepherders’ Ball still held during the winter. One attraction of these dances was the presence of young Basque girls who had come over to work in the hotel as maids and waitresses. Turnover was rapid because most of the young women quickly received marriage proposals.

Many weddings were performed at the Star, and the Jaureguis would furnish the wedding supper and dance as a wedding gift to the happy couples. In the years that followed the marriages, the Star served as a lying-in hospital for expectant mothers who came in from remote sheep camps and ranches where they lived. Matilde Jauregui, the wife of the owner, assisted the doctor with deliveries and care of the mothers and their new babies.

Also, during World War I, a flu epidemic raged, and many stricken people were cared for at the Star. Board and room during the early years cost $1.00 a day, and drinks at the bar were eight to ten for $1.00. During Prohibition, drinks were served in a private room where the evidence could be quickly hidden in the event of a raid.

Meals were served family-style, in the patterned, copper ceiling dining room. When the meals were ready, a waitress rang a large bell which could be heard everywhere in the hotel. There were no menus, and everyone ate the same thing at long tables where they mingled while eating. Meals included porru-salda (leek soup), baratzuri-salda (garlic soup), bacaloa a la Vizcaina (salt cod in tomato and pimento sauce), clams and rice, garbanzos with chorizos, arroz con polio (rice with chicken), rice pudding and flan or fruit. Spaghetti and beans were added as side dishes. Most of the early diners were boarders of the hotel.

Family style service and the calling dinner bell are customs still practiced today. There are some long- term boarders who are considered family and who eat at the Star, but most of the restaurant business comes from the community and tourism. Jauregui, Corta, Arrascada, Garamendi, Bengoa, Ozamis, Juaristi, Esnoz, Yanci, Aldazabal, Sarasua, Leonis, Lazcano. These were families making the Star the only hotel in Elko continuously owned by Basques, carrying on a 100+ year tradition of Basque hospitality.

The present proprietor of the Star Hotel is Scott Ygoa. He purchased the establishment in November of 2004 and is continuing to provide the friendly atmosphere and excellent food that has been a hallmark of the Star since 1910."

text:
More than 35 million years ago, an enormous volcanic eruption helped shape a mountain range in West Texas. Today, one of the state's most remote roads takes you right through the surrounding landscape.

It's called Pinto Canyon Road, and it runs between Marfa and Ruidosa, near the Mexican border.

Most people associate West Texas with wide-open desert, but the Chinati Mountains tell a different geological story.

The mountains were shaped by one of the largest volcanic eruptions in the region's history. Over millions of years, erosion exposed layers of rock and helped create the rugged peaks and canyons you see today.

Pinto Canyon Road offers a chance to see that landscape up close.

The route begins south of Marfa on Ranch Road 2810, crossing miles of open ranchland before reaching the mountains. Eventually, the pavement gives way to dirt and gravel, and the road winds through increasingly rugged terrain.

It's a part of Texas that looks very different from the Hill Country, the Gulf Coast, or the plains of North Texas.

And getting there requires some preparation.

Cell service is unreliable, portions of the road are rough, and rain can make the route dangerous. A high-clearance vehicle with good tires is recommended. Bring extra water, carry offline maps, and check conditions before setting out.

The nearby Chinati Mountains State Natural Area covers nearly 39,000 acres, although it isn't open to the public yet. For now, Pinto Canyon Road offers one of the best ways to appreciate this unusual landscape.

I've spent a lot of time researching places across Texas, and I'm continually surprised by how much there is to discover beyond the destinations everyone already knows.

That's a big part of what I write about in my newsletter. Places you might never have considered visiting, along with the history that makes them interesting.

text:
I have been on search committees and on tenure and promotion committees. From those who are invited for campus interviews, I'd say women are favored over men, but perhaps not by much. However, being white is sometimes a hindrance. 

I was university tenure committee head twice at my U (University of North Georgia). I honestly don't think there was any favoritism of males or females. We mostly counted publications. Sometimes extremely bad teaching was taken into account.

My one experience that soured me was when we had 3 candidates for a job. Two white guys and a Chinese woman. One of the white guys was not a fully developed academic. The other was great. Easy to talk to. Easy to relate to. Very good publications, but his previous job had been at a U where "very good" was not nearly good enough. Seemed like an excellent colleague, which was what I had told the department head was what we were looking for.

I could not get the Chinese woman to talk about economics (our field) for the life of me. I tried repeatedly, but she would not engage. So for me it was no question.

My department had had assured me that he would take the search committee's recommendation. The result was one strong recommendation for the white guy and one weak recommendation for the Chinese woman.

The DH thought it would be great for our students to get the perspective of the Chinese woman. I chewed him out thoroughly. He offered to resign.

The Chinese woman ended up being the best publisher in the entire school of business. 18 refereed journal publications in 5 years (our minimum is 2, and few faculty members have 5). But they were all coauthored with her Chinese friends at other universities or were solo authored.

We did not hire a colleague. But administrators like to brag, so they were happy.
